title: Niharika @ Neha vs Meenu Verma on 28 September, 2018
full_text: Niharika @ Neha vs Meenu Verma on 28 September, 2018 IN THE COURT OF SHRI PUNEET NAGPAL, MM (NI ACT)-01, SOUTH-WEST DISTRICT: NEW DELHI Old CC no.6258/14 New CC no.4994178/16 Under Section 138 of N.I. Act In the matter of: NIHARIKA @ NEHA w/o Shri Ashok Kumar R/o A 14, Suraj Vihar, Dwarka More, Kakrola, New Delhi. ... Complainant Versus MEENU VERMA w/o Shri Sandeep Verma r/o Flat no.106, Pocket III, Sector 11, DDA, SFS Flats, Dwarka, New Delhi. ... Accused Date of Institution : 02.07.2014 Date on which judgment was reserved : 27.08.2016 Date of Judgment : 29.09.2018 JUDGMENT 1. Shorn off unnecessary details, the case of the complainant as narrated in the complaint is that the complainant was known to one Ankita Choudhary for more 6-7 years and the said Ankita Choudhary had introduced the accused to the Old CC no.6258/14 New CC no.4994178/16 NIHARIKA @ NEHA VS MEENU VERMA complainant and thereafter, the accused and the complainant developed friendly relations. It has been averred in the complaint in the month of April 2014, the accused had come to the house of complainant alongwith Ankita, Sudha and Rakhi. There, the accused convinced the complainant that her father-in-law was associated with big construction houses and the accused was also assisting him in the business. It was communicated by the accused to the complainant that the construction company with which her father-in-law is associated, is launching a new project wherein, if one invests, one can easily earn a good profit in few months. For the same, the accused expressed her desire to the complainant that she requires sum of Rs.11 lacs. It was also promised by the accused that in case, the complainant advances Rs.11 lacs, the accused shall repay sum of Rs.12 lacs. Initially, the complainant was not convinced and refused to advance any money. However, on the asking and assurance of the accused, the complainant agreed. Relying on the assurances of the accused, and after the accused had shown some stamp papers, the complainant arranged sum of Rs.10,72,000/- from her mother and advanced the same to the accused in three installments of Rs.72,000/-, Rs.5 lacs and Rs.5 lacs each. At the time of advancement of loan, the accused executed a receipt cum declaration of Rs.5 lacs in favour of the complainant, wherein Ankita, Sudha and Rakhi signed as witnesses. The same has been exhibited as Ex.CW1/1. At the time of execution Ex.CW1/1, the accused also issued a blank cheque bearing no.266616 drawn on account number 913010056243198 with AXIS Bank, Dwarka, New Delhi as a security. Subsequently, when the complainant Old CC no.6258/14 New CC no.4994178/16 NIHARIKA @ NEHA VS MEENU VERMA demanded the repayment of above stated amount, the accused requested for some more time. That finally in discharge of her legal liability, the accused issued three cheques for sum of Rs.12 lacs (cumulatively). Out of those three cheques, the complainant presented one cheque bearing no.266615 dated 06.05.2014 for Rs.5 lacs drawn on AXIS Bank, Dwarka, New Delhi (hereinafter called as cheque in question) (Ex.CW1/3) to the complainant and assured the complainant that the cheque shall be honoured at the time of its presentation. Accordingly, as per the instructions of the accused, the complainant presented the cheque in question for encashment on 19.05.2014 which to the despair of the complainant, got dishonoured on presentation with the remarks ''Funds Insufficient'' vide cheque return memo dated 19.05.2014 (Ex.CW1/4). This constrained the complainant to send a legal notice dated 02.06.2014 (Ex.CW1/5) to the accused. The said legal notice was received back by the complainant with the remarks 'No person by the name of Meenu Verma is residing at this address'. It has been averred in the complaint that the accused had deliberately avoided the service of legal demand notice and therefore, the legal notice is deemed to have been served. Thereafter, the complainant filed the present complaint. 2 Cognizance of the offence under Section 138 NI Act was taken against the accused and summons were issued. The accused entered appearance. Notice under Section 251 CrPC was framed against the accused to which she pleaded not guilty. In his plea of defence, recorded on 10.04.2015, the accused Old CC no.6258/14 New CC no.4994178/16 NIHARIKA @ NEHA VS MEENU VERMA submitted that the cheque in question was issued in blank signed condition to the complainant as security for the purpose of committee / chit fund. EVIDENCE OF THE COMPLAINANT 3. In Post Summoning Evidence, the complainant chose to examine herself as sole complainant's witness and appeared as CW1 and adopted her Pre-Summoning Evidence tendered by way of affidavit Ex.CW1/A. The accused had filed an application under Section 145(2) NI Act and the accused was allowed to cross examine the complainant. 4. In her cross examination, the complainant brought on record copies of her passbook for the bank account maintained by her with Oriental Bank of Commerce and with State Bank of India. The same are Ex.CW1/D1 and Ex.CW1/D2. The complainant deposed in her cross-examination that she had met the father- in- law of the accused and she wanted to complain against the accused as the accused had failed to repay the loan amount. It was also deposed by the complainant that the declaration Ex.CW1/1, was got prepared by the accused herself and that she had only appended her signatures. The complainant deposed that the source of her income of Rs.50,000/- per month approximately was rental income. The complainant also admitted that apart from the cheques which have been placed on record, she is having possession of one other cheque, issued by the accused, and the same was for amount of Rs.4 lacs. The Old CC no.6258/14 New CC no.4994178/16 NIHARIKA @ NEHA VS MEENU VERMA complainant deposed that the money which was taken by her from her mother and which was used to advance the loan, was taken in cash. The complainant categorically denied the suggestion that the cheque in question was issued as security for chit fund / committee. The complainant, however, admitted, that she had advanced sum of Rs.4.5 lacs to one Kanti, Rs.7 lacs to Sudha, Rs.6 lacs to Ankita and approximately Rs.9 lacs to Rakhi. DEFENCE OF THE ACCUSED 5 The version of facts as discernible from the plea of defence recorded at the stage of framing of notice under Section 251 CrPC, from cross-examination of complainant CW1, from statement of accused recorded under Section 313 CrPC are that the accused has admitted that the cheque in question bears her signatures. However, the defence of the accused is that the cheque in question was not handed over by the accused to the complainant for making any repayment of loan amount. But the same was handed over as security as the complainant was running a chit fund / committee. The accused has also denied the factum of having executed any receipt cum declaration Ex.CW1/1. 6. Accused chose to examine herself as sole defence witness and appeared as DW1. In her testimony, the accused deposed that the complainant was running committee / chit fund since year 2012 and that she alongwith Sudha, Rakhi, Ankita, Rekha, Poonam had started in investing in such committees. For Old CC no.6258/14 New CC no.4994178/16 NIHARIKA @ NEHA VS MEENU VERMA the same, the accused had handed over to blank cheques to the complainant as security. The accused had denied having taken any loan from the complainant and also denied the factum of execution of Ex.CW1/1. It is pertinent to mention that despite opportunity, the complainant has failed to cross examine the accused / DW1 and therefore, the testimony of the accused has gone unrebutted. 7. It is pertinent to mention here that though both the parties had cited name of Ankita Choudhary, who was a witness to the transactions that took place between them, however, nor the complainant and neither the accused had summoned Ankita Choudhary as witness. Therefore, the court had summoned Ankita Choudhary as court witness by exercising powers under section 311 CrPC with the objective of discerning the true nature of transaction that took place between the parties. 8. The said Ankita Choudhary appeared as court witness no.01 and deposed that she knew both the complainant and the accused. She deposed that she had appended her signatures on Ex.CW1/1. However, at the time of appending signatures, the paper was blank. At the same time, the court witness deposed that the complainant was actually running a committee and that she was also a member of such committee. It was the version of the witness that the complainant used to take cheques from the members of the committee and it might be the case that the accused may also have handed over the cheques in question to the complainant as a security in respect of Old CC no.6258/14 New CC no.4994178/16 NIHARIKA @ NEHA VS MEENU VERMA committee. As the court witness had deposed in favour of accused and against the complainant, an opportunity to cross examine the court witness was afforded to the complainant. 9. The court witness was cross examined at instance of complainant. In her cross-examination, the court witness admitted that the complainant has filed a complaint against her under section 138 NI Act and the same is pending in Dwarka Courts. It was also admitted by the court witness that she had filed a complaint against the complainant in police station Dwarka South wherein, she had mentioned that she was having financial transaction with the complainant. The witness also deposed that the complainant has filed a false case against her in respect of dishonour of some cheques, which were handed over to the complainant in respect of some informal committee / chit fund and that the complainant has misused those cheques by filing a false complaint against the court witness. The court witness categorically denied that she was deposing falsely at the instance of the accused as she was hostile towards the complainant. 10. The factual position being thus, now let us quickly run through the legal benchmark which is to be satisfied in order to constitute an offence u/s 138 NI Act-: (i) that the person must have drawn a cheque on an account maintained by him in a bank for payment of certain amount of money to another person from out of that account. (ii) that a cheque should have been issued for discharge, in whole or in part, or any debt or other liability. Old CC no.6258/14 New CC no.4994178/16 NIHARIKA @ NEHA VS MEENU VERMA (iii) that the cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it was drawn or within the period of its validity whichever is earlier. (iv) that cheque is returned by the bank unpaid because of the amount of money standing to the credit of the account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with the bank. (v) that the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque makes a demand for the payment of said amount of money by giving a notice in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, within 30 days of the receipt of the information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid. (vi) the drawer of the said cheque fails to make payment of the said amount of money to the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque within 15 days of the receipt of the said notice. 11. Being cumulative, it goes without saying that it is only when, all the aforementioned ingredients are satisfied, that a person who had drawn the cheque can be deemed to have committed an offence under Section 138 of the NI Act. 12. In the present case, the accused has admitted that the cheque in question was handed over to the complainant in a blank signed condition. However, it is defence of the accused that the same was handed over to the complainant as the complainant was running an informal committee system and the accused was one of such members. 13. File perused and submissions heard. Let us determine, whether the accused has succeeded in establishing various defence taken by her. The accused has denied the Old CC no.6258/14 New CC no.4994178/16 NIHARIKA @ NEHA VS MEENU VERMA receipt of legal demand notice and therefore, the parties are at variance on two primary issues. Firstly, whether the legal demand notice was validly issued to the accused and secondly, whether the cheque in question was issued to discharge legal liability towards the complainant. SERVICE OF LEGAL DEMAND NOTICE 14. Let us begin by examining first, the much hackneyed and cliched defence of non service of legal notice. Perusal of the file shows that the legal notice which was sent by the complainant by way of speed post and through courier were delivered back to the complainant with the report "'Meena Kumari is not residing at the address furnished by the complainant''. Therefore, it has been contended on behalf of the accused that admittedly the legal notice was never received by the accused and therefore, offence u/s 138 N.I Act is not made out against the accused as non service of legal notice strikes at the very edifice of the maintainability of a complaint u/s 138 NI Act. On the other hand, Ld. Counsel for the complainant has argued that the accused herself had a role to play in the non receipt of legal notice as she deliberately refused to receive the legal notice and, therefore, the accused cannot be allowed to shield herself behind the technical objection of non receipt of legal notice and claim immunity from prosecution in respect of offence u/s 138 NI Act. 15. This defence of the accused has to fail for more than Old CC no.6258/14 New CC no.4994178/16 NIHARIKA @ NEHA VS MEENU VERMA one reason. Though, accused argues that legal demand notice was sent on wrong address, but quite notably, has not disputed the correctness of her address as appearing on the legal notice Ex. CW1/8 and Ex.CW1/9. No evidence has been led by the accused to support, much less proof her submission that the legal notice which was issued by the complainant, was issued on wrong address. Thus, the address on the legal notice Ex. CW1/8 and Ex.CW1/9 once having been shown to be correct address of the accused, in such circumstances, a mere denial of the service of legal notice would not ipso facto rebut the presumption of due service. 16. At the same time, quite notably, the accused has not disputed the correctness of her address as appearing on the legal notice during her testimony as DW1. This address on the legal notice once having been shown to be correct address of the accused and the legal notice having been dispatched by registered post, a presumption of due service arises (in view of Section 27 of General Clauses Act and Section 114 of Indian Evidence Act) and now it was incumbent on the accused to lead evidence to prove that the notice was sent to her on wrong address. Not even an iota of evidence has been brought on record by the accused to displace the presumption of due service. In any event, in view of the authoritative Judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court in C.C. Alavi Haji vs Palapetty Muhadmmed and Ors. (2007) 6 SCC 555, the rigour of the requirement of service of legal notice has been reduced to an almost vanishing point in Section 138 NI Act jurisprudence. The Hon'ble Supreme Court Old CC no.6258/14 New CC no.4994178/16 NIHARIKA @ NEHA VS MEENU VERMA while discussing the true intent behind the service of legal demand notice as a precursor to the launch of prosecution has quite categorically held that the service of summons of the court is opportunity enough for the accused to pay the cheque amount and evade prosecution, any accused who fails to pay the amount within 15 days of the service of summons, clearly cannot shield himself behind the technical demand of non service of legal notice. The relevant extract of the decision deserves to be quoted in extenso :- ''17. It is also to be borne in mind that the requirement of giving of notice is a clear departure from the rule of criminal law, where there is no stipulation of giving of a notice before filing a complaint. Any drawer who claims that he did not receive the notice sent by post, can, within 15 days of receipt of summons from the court in respect of the complaint under Section 138 of Act, make payment of the cheque amount and submits to the court that he had made payment within 15 days of receipt of summons (by receiving a copy of complaint with the summons) and, therefore, the complaint is liable to be rejected. A person who does not pay within 15 days of receipt of the summons from the court alongwith the copy of the complaint under Section 138 of the Act, cannot obviously contend that there was no proper service of notice as required under Section 138 , by ignoring statutory presumption to the contrary under Section 27 of the G.C.Act and Section 114 of the Evidence Act. In our view, any other interpretation of the proviso, would defeat the very object of the legislation''. 17. The non service of legal notice challenge having been met, let us now turn to the core issue in this case and Old CC no.6258/14 New CC no.4994178/16 NIHARIKA @ NEHA VS MEENU VERMA examine ''whether the cheque in question can be said to have been issued in discharge of legal liability or not''. EXISTENCE OF LEGALLY ENFORCEABLE DEBT OR LIABILITY. 18. Let us again briefly recapitulate that the accused has admitted having drawn the cheque in question on a bank account maintained in her name and having signed the same. Once these foundational facts are admitted and a factual base is established, presumption of the cheque having been issued in discharge of legally sustainable liability and drawn for good consideration arises by virtue of Section 118 (a) and Section 139 of NI Act. 19. As per the scheme of the NI Act , on proof of foundational facts, a presumption arises as to the cheque having been issued in discharge of a legal liability and the burden is on the accused to rebut the said presumption. This clearly is an instance of the rule of ''reverse onus'' in action where it is incumbent on the accused to lead what can be called as ''negative evidence''. Evidence of a character, not to prove a fact affirmatively, but to lead evidence to show non existence of liability. Keeping in view, that this is a departure from the cardinal rule of ''presumption of innocence'' in favour of the accused, and also keeping in mind that the negative evidence is not easy to be led by its very nature. It is now fairly settled that the accused can rebut this presumption on a scale of preponderance of probabilities. Lack of consideration or a legally enforceable debt Old CC no.6258/14 New CC no.4994178/16 NIHARIKA @ NEHA VS MEENU VERMA need not be proved to the hilt or beyond all reasonable doubts. Preponderance is superiority in weight. Preponderance of probabilities, simply put means more probably than not and superior in evidentiary weight than the opposite. 20. In 'Rangappa vs Sri Mohan (2010) 11 SCC 441, a three judge bench observed that Section 139 of the NI Act, is stated to be an example of a reverse onus clause which is in tune with the legislator intent of improving the credibility of Negotiable Instruments. Section 138 of the NI Act provides for speedy remedy in a criminal forum, in relation to the dishonour of the cheque. In case of Kumar Exports vs. Sharma Carpets , (2009) 2 SCC 513, the Hon'ble Supreme Court had held:- 'The accused under Section 138 NI Act has two options. He can either show that the consideration and debt did not exit or that under the particular circumstances of the case, the non existence of consideration and debt is so probable that a prudent man ought to suppose that no consideration and debt existed. To rebut the statutory presumption, an accused is not expected to prove his defence beyond reasonable doubt as it is expected of the complainant in a criminal trial. The accused may adduce direct evidence to prove that the note in question was not supported by consideration and that there was no debt or liability to be discharged by him. However, the court need not insist in every case that the accused should disprove the non existence of consideration and debt by leading direct evidence because the existence of negative evidence is neither possible nor contemplated. At the same time, it is clear that bare denial of the passing of the consideration and existence of debt, apparently would not serve the purpose of the accused. Old CC no.6258/14 New CC no.4994178/16 NIHARIKA @ NEHA VS MEENU VERMA Something which his probable has to be brought on record for getting the burden of proof shifted to the complainant. To disprove the presumptions, the accused should bring on record such facts and circumstances, upon consideration of which, the court may either believe that the consideration and debt did not exist or there non existence was so probably that a prudent man under the circumstances of the case, act upon the plea that they did not exist. Apart from adducing direct evidence to prove that the note in question, was not supported by consideration or that he had not incurred any debt or liability, the accused may also rely upon the circumstantial evidence and if the circumstances so relied upon are so compelling, the burden may likewise shift again on the complainant. The accused may also rely upon presumptions of fact, for instance, those mentioned in Section 114 of the Evidence Act to rebut the presumptions arises under Section 118 and 139 of NI Act''. 21. As discussed above, it is clear that the accused need not discharge his or her liability beyond the shadow of reasonable doubt. He just needs to create holes in the case, set out by the complaint. Accused can say that the version brought forth by the complainant is inherently unbelievable and therefore, the prosecution cannot stand. Or the accused can give his version of the story and say that on the basis of his version, the story of the complainant cannot be believed. In the first situation, the accused has nothing to do except to point inherent inconsistencies in the version of the complainant. 22 So far as the factum of liability is concerned, in view of the mandatory presumptions of law as discussed above, if an Old CC no.6258/14 New CC no.4994178/16 NIHARIKA @ NEHA VS MEENU VERMA accepted signed cheque has been produced the complainant, then there cannot be any inherent lacuna in the existence of the liability. But then, definitely, accused can create some loopholes in the story of the complainant by impeaching the credit of the witness during cross examination. Accused can discharge his burden by demonstrating the preponderance of probabilities coming in its way. 23 Coming to the facts of the present case, it has been contended on behalf of the accused that accused has never taken the alleged loan of Rs.10,72,000/- from the complainant and therefore, no occasion arises for the issuance of cheque in question for sum of Rs.5 lacs to the complainant for discharging any liability to partially repay the alleged amount of Rs.10,72,000/-. Perusal of the file shows that the complainant who is the sole complainant witness has been cross-examined at length at the instance of the accused to create doubts on the version of events as have been testified by the complainant and to prove the defence taken by the accused. Let us determine, whether the accused has succeeded in creating doubts in the version of the complainant. 24 To begin with, the Ld. Counsel for the accused has argued that the version of the complainant as is discernible from the affidavit Ex.CW1/A filed in lieu of examination-in-chief, is that, the complainant has taken the whole amount of Rs.10,72,000/- from her mother Mrs. Promila and had used the said money to advance the loan amount to the accused. Old CC no.6258/14 New CC no.4994178/16 NIHARIKA @ NEHA VS MEENU VERMA However, the accused has failed to examine her mother to prove and substantiate her assertion of arranging the loan amount from her mother. It has been submitted on behalf of the accused that as per the version of the complainant, the accused had taken the entire amount from her mother in cash, and the complainant has failed to bring even to bring an iota of evidence on record to prove that the mother of the complainant was financially competent / capable of advancing such an humongous amount of Rs.10,72,000/- to the complainant. Therefore, Ld. Counsel for the accused has argued that adverse inference ought to be drawn against the complainant as the complainant has failed to lead any evidence much less cogent to show that she was capable of advancing the alleged loan amount to the accused. 25. At the same time, it has been contended on behalf of the accused that the fact that the complainant has herself admitted that the whole sum of Rs.10,72,000/- was taken by her from her mother which was used to advance the alleged loan clearly shows that the complainant was neither capable nor was in possession of sufficient funds to advance such a huge loan and thus, this in itself, raises questions on the financial capacity / competency of the complainant to advance the alleged loan amount. 26 Ld. Counsel for the accused has implored the court that considering the financial background of the complainant, the amount of Rs.10,72,000/- is quite high and therefore, the Old CC no.6258/14 New CC no.4994178/16 NIHARIKA @ NEHA VS MEENU VERMA capacity of the complainant, in advancing such huge amount be delved deeper and scrutinized arduously. 27 Ld. Counsel for the accused has referred to the cross- examination of the complainant done at the instance of the accused and has submitted that the complainant has herself stated in her cross-examination that she has given Rs.4.5 lacs to one Kanti, Rs.6 lacs to one Ankita, Rs.9 lacs to one Rakhi and Rs.7 lacs to one Sudha. It has been contended on behalf of the accused that if the testimony of the complainant, is accepted as gospel truth, it emerges that the complainant was having a huge cash amount running into millions. However, there is not even an iota of evidence, much less cogent, which could support this fact of the complainant having financial resources / competency of having such humongous cash amount in her possession. 28 Per contra, Ld. Counsel for the complainant has argued that at the time of advancement of loan, the accused had executed a declaration note which has been exhibited as Ex.CW1/1 and which clearly proves the factum of advancement of loan of Rs.5 lacs to the accused. However, Ld. counsel for the accused has argued that though the accused has categorically denied the factum of having executed Ex.CW1/1. At the same time, the falsity of the case projected by the complainant is also proved through the testimony of court witness Ms Ankita Choudhary. It has been submitted on behalf of the accused that the court witness has categorically testified that she had appended her signatures on Ex.CW1/1. However, when the Old CC no.6258/14 New CC no.4994178/16 NIHARIKA @ NEHA VS MEENU VERMA signatures were appended on Ex.CW1/1 by court witness Ankita Choudhary, the document was a blank paper. Therefore, it was contended on behalf of the accused that this clearly proves that accused has not executed the Declaration Ex.CW1/1. 29. In response to the above stated argument advanced on behalf of the accused, Ld. Counsel for the complainant has submitted that the court witness is an 'interested witness', and she has every reason to depose falsely against the complainant as the complainant has filed a complaint against the said court witness also. Therefore, ld. Counsel for the complainant has argued that the testimony of the court witness is not reliable and ought to be eschewed from consideration. However, I am not in concurrence with the above stated argument advanced on behalf of the accused. Mere fact that the complainant has filed a complaint against the court witness, does not ipso facto, lead to a conclusion that the court witness is deposing falsely. Therefore, I am inclined to accept the testimony of the court witness and in my opinion, Ex.CW1/1 is a forged and fabricated document and the same cannot be relied upon. 30 In my opinion, the argument of Ld. Counsel for the accused questioning the financial competency / prowess, of the complainant, is worthy of acceptance as it is quite normal for ordinary prudent person to remain assiduous and watchful while humoring into financial transaction. In the ordinary course of human nature, money matters are considered sensitive enough to demand alert and attentive attendance of human psyche. The Old CC no.6258/14 New CC no.4994178/16 NIHARIKA @ NEHA VS MEENU VERMA degree of alertness and attentiveness, gets bigger and sharper with the increase in the amount and the fragile financial status of the lender which are inversely proportional to each other. In the present case, when a huge amount of money has been alleged to have been advanced, its all natural for the complainant to come forth with reliable and credible evidence. It appears quite indigestible and implausible to believe that the complainant would advance loan to the tune of Rs.10,72,000/- especially when the complainant herself is not having possession of such an humongous sum, but she had to borrow the same from her mother. 31. The suspicion on the version of events, deposed by the complainant, gets further murkier on perusal of the cross- examination of the complainant, wherein the complainant has herself stated that at the time of advancement of sum of Rs.5 lacs, the accused had issued a blank signed cheque bearing no.266616 to the complainant as a security (The said cheque is also on record). As per the version of events, deposed by the complainant, the cheque in question was advanced subsequent to the above stated blank signed security cheque after expiry of time period of 15 days in terms of the agreement arrived at between the parties, in pursuance of which the loan in question was advanced. It is pertinent to mention that the cheque in question bears the number 266615 and the other cheque bears the number 266616. Therefore, in the ordinary course of nature, the cheque in question must have been issued by the accused prior in time before the advancement of the other cheque Old CC no.6258/14 New CC no.4994178/16 NIHARIKA @ NEHA VS MEENU VERMA bearing no.266616, which was issued as a security cheque in a blank signed condition at the time of advancement of the alleged amount of Rs.5 lacs. Therefore, grave suspicion arises on the version of events deposed by the complainant. 32. At the same time, the testimony of the accused wherein the accused has deposed that she was a member of a committee which was being run by the complainant and that the cheque in question was issued as a security in respect of such committee, has gone unrebutted and un-controverted as the complainant has failed to cross examine accused. It is a settled law that unrebutted testimony of any witness, has to be accepted at its face value. 33. It is significant to mention that the fiction of friendly loan is very easy to be weaved, conceived and averred but very hard to be proved and establish. It becomes very captious when stakes are high and stands of the parties are fiercely and frantically brought forth with equal force and fortitude. In the present case, as per the assertions and avernments of the complainant, the accused had demanded the loan amount in the month of April 2014 and the same was advanced by the complainant in April 2014 itself. The complainant had admitted in her cross examination that she had taken the entire sum from her mother and the same was used to advance loan to the accused. In her cross examination, the complainant testified that she had also advanced other loans running into lakhs to at least four other persons. However, the Old CC no.6258/14 New CC no.4994178/16 NIHARIKA @ NEHA VS MEENU VERMA complainant has failed to bring even an iota of evidence to prove her assertion of arranging the entire loan amount from her mother Ms Promila. A bare perusal of the avernments made by the complainant in affidavit Ex.CW1/A and her cross- examination, clearly shows that by no stretch of imagination, it can be concluded that the complainant was in possession of cash amount of Rs.11 lacs approximately with her at the time of advancement of loan. 34 In 'K. Subramani vs K. Damodar Naidu ' 2015, Civil Courts Cases 001 (SC), the Hon'ble Apex Court found the requirement of the complainant to establish his financial capacity to lend money relevant in cases under Section 138 of NI Act. Reliance in this regard can also be placed on the Judgment of Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in the matter titled as Satish Kumar vs State of Delhi 2013, VIII AD (Delhi) 465, in which it has been held as follows:- "This Court finds some merits in the observations made by Ld. ASJ that the petitioner had not been able to prove any three sources of money. Though, he had specifically mentioned the same in his deposition. In fact, failure on his part to prove any entry in his bank account showing withdrawal of any amount during the relevant period, created a reasonable doubt about the consideration for the cheuqe in question.............''. ''.....................however, once burden of proof is shifted back to the petitioner / complainant, he was unable to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt by establishing the source of alleged friendly loan extended to respondent no.02, thus dis-entitling him to grant of relief on basis of the Negotiable Old CC no.6258/14 New CC no.4994178/16 NIHARIKA @ NEHA VS MEENU VERMA Instruments.................''. 35. In a criminal trial under Section 138 of the NI Act, it is all necessary that the execution of the cheque against the alleged loan should be proved with evidence of irrevocable nature and impeccable character. Mere production of the cheque cannot made the case of the complainant sacrosanct and absolute so as to exempt in from all blemishes and burden. It is trite to say that the cheque as an instrument is very prone to be misused and thus it becomes all necessary for the complainant to come up with cogent and convincing evidence to win over the confidence of the court. 36. Therefore, in the light of the above discussion, the theory of handing over of the loan, does not inspire confidence. The complainant has failed to prove the alleged source of funds or her overall financial prowess / competency before the court as she has failed to prove her assertion that she was having ready cash amount of Rs.11 lacs with her at the time when the loan was demanded by the accused. At the same time, failure of the complainant to examine her mother to prove the fact of having taken sum of Rs.10,72,000/- from her also renders the friendly loan story unworthy of credence. 37. On the other hand, Ld. Counsel for the complainant has laboured hard to pick holes into the defence of the accused by submitting that accused has failed to prove her defence that the cheque in question was issued as a security cheque as the Old CC no.6258/14 New CC no.4994178/16 NIHARIKA @ NEHA VS MEENU VERMA accused was the member of a committee / chit fund which was being run by the complainant. It has been argued that the accused has failed to bring any plausible evidence to prove the defence taken by her. 38. It is a settled position of law that the case of the complainant should stand on its own leg. It cannot take advantage of the weakness of the defence, nor can the court, on its own, make out a new case for the prosecution and convict the accused on that basis. If defence version is incorrect, it does not mean the prosecution version is necessarily correct. Therefore, the contention of Ld. Counsel for the complainant regarding the weak defence of the accused appears to be of no use in sailing through the case of the complainant as accused has made decisive intrusion into the case built up by the complainant by successfully pointing out towards the inherently incurable defects into the web of facts weaved by the complainant. 39. The Hon'ble Apex Court in the epic Judgment passed in the case titled as 'Sharad Birdichand Sarda vs State of Maharasthra' (1984) 4 SCC 116, while discussing the principles of appreciation of prosecution and defence evidence, has held that- ''It is well settled that the prosecution must stand or fall on its own legs and it cannot derive any strength from the weakness of the defence. This is trite law. However, where various links in a chain are in themselves complete, then a false plea or false defence may be called into aid only to lend assurance Old CC no.6258/14 New CC no.4994178/16 NIHARIKA @ NEHA VS MEENU VERMA to the court. In other words, before using the additional link it must be proved that all the links in the chain are complete and do not suffer from any infirmity. It is not the law that where there is any infirmity or lacuna in the prosecution case, the same could be cured or supplied by a false defence or a plea which is not accepted by a court''. 40. It is all more significant that presumption can only be raised in furtherance of prosecution case and not in derogation of the same. The three judge bench of Hon'ble Supreme Court in a case dealing with prevention of Corruption Act has observed in respect of presumption of law in '' Trilok Chand Jain vs State of Delhi ', 1977 AIR 666 as under:- ''The presumption therefore, can be used in furtherance of the prosecution case and not in derogation of it. If the story set up by the prosecution inherently militates against or is inconsistent with the fact presumed, the presumption will be rendered sterile from its inception''. 41 Thus, in view of the totality of the circumstance and the settled legal positions as discussed above, the case attempted to be built by the complainant, appears to be suffering from fatal infirmities so much so, it goes directly to the root of the case and shakes the very edifice on which the case of the complainant rests. It is also relevant to mention here that it is of paramount importance to demand evidence of unambiguous, impeccable and of unimpeachable in nature so as to entail criminal conviction of the accused and which Old CC no.6258/14 New CC no.4994178/16 NIHARIKA @ NEHA VS MEENU VERMA the complainant has failed to bring. 42 In the case of 'Kulvinder Singh vs Kafeel Ahmad'', Crl L. P. 478 of 2011, decided on 04.01.2013, Hon'ble Delhi High Court has held that the basic principle in criminal law is that the guilt of the accused / respondent, must be proved beyond reasonable doubts and if there is any slightest doubt about the commission of an offence, then the benefit has to accrue to him. 43 At the same time, it is important to underscore the established canon of criminal law that in order to pass a conviction in a criminal case, the accused ''must be'' guilty and not merely ''may be'' guilty. The mental distance between ''may be'' guilty to ''must be'' guilty is a long one and must be travel not on surmises and conjectures, but by cogent evidence. In this case, after the accused successfully rebutted the presumption of consideration by raising a doubt on the very factum of the loan. The accused has clearly presented a case which is superior in way. And as per the settled law, this is all that what is required, as preponderance of probabilities is not a rigorous standard of proof, but only so much evidence as makes the court lean in, in favour of one side and not the other. Consequently, the benefit of doubt must go to the accused. The material on record does not suggest that the accused ''must be'' guilty whichever way one looks at it. Old CC no.6258/14 New CC no.4994178/16 NIHARIKA @ NEHA VS MEENU VERMA 44. In view of the above discussions, the present case appears to be a fit case where benefit of doubt can be extended to the accused. Accordingly, in view of the above discussions, I hold that the complainant has failed to prove his case. The accused has been able to rebut presumption under Section 118 and 139 NI Act arising in favour of the complainant. 45 In the light of the foregoing reasons, it is clear that the accused Meenu Verma has succeeded in rebutting the presumption of legal liability and the complainant has failed to prove the same affirmatively.
